Sixty Days, No Deadline, and a Strait That Stopped Moving

On August 17, the 60-day period in the U.S.-Iran memorandum expired. Tehran’s response was to deny that it had ever existed.

Iranian Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmail Baghaei said the memorandum contained no clause titled “60-day deadline.” It only set a 60-day period for discussions on sanctions relief and the nuclear file, he said, with room for an extension. 

Because Washington had allegedly violated the agreement within weeks of its signing, Baghaei argued, the talks never began and the entire deadline question had become irrelevant. 

That is one way to end a deadline: declare it legally imaginary after it arrives.

Another Iranian official told Reuters that Tehran has moved from a defensive posture to a “fully offensive” one. Iran has given the United States a few weeks to implement the memorandum in full, the official said, and will consider a “timely and precise” military action to break the U.S. naval blockade if diplomacy fails. The deadline does not exist. Iran has simply replaced it with its own. 

The immediate battlefield is Hormuz. Ship-tracking firm Kpler recorded five commodity vessels crossing the strait on Saturday and none on Sunday, versus 31 during the preceding weekend.

 This is not an Iranian declaration of control or an American declaration of control. It is commercial shipping voting with its engines. 

Iran says the strait will reopen only when the United States meets its obligations under the Islamabad memorandum. 

It is still negotiating with Oman on a mechanism that, Tehran says, would respect the sovereignty of both Iran and Oman while allowing commercial traffic to transit safely. 

The proposed formula has all the usual regional ingredients: sovereignty, security, mediation and somebody else’s oil.

A report in the Wall Street Journal says Arab intelligence officials have detected a strategic shift among Iran’s hardliners, who are preparing for a wider war and increasingly discussing offensive action inside enemy territory. 

Options reportedly include disrupting Gulf internet cables, inciting unrest among Shia communities in Gulf states and even a ground operation against Kuwait.

That is the map of a regime trying to compensate for military pressure by making smaller neighbors feel the cost first.

The United States, meanwhile, is considering what Bloomberg described as unprecedented economic pressure: sanctions on Chinese financial firms and money-exchange companies linked to Iran, plus further freezes on Iranian assets abroad.

Washington’s wider blockade plans reportedly depend on cooperation from Iraq, Turkey, Pakistan, Afghanistan, Turkmenistan, Azerbaijan and Armenia. 

Two of those states, Turkey and Pakistan, signed the Mecca defense pact with Saudi Arabia days ago. The region is assembling overlapping security systems while everyone checks whether their names appear on the next sanctions list.

The new Middle East order is finally becoming self-reliant.
Everyone is now responsible for everyone else’s war.

Trump: Iran, Oman, Gaza, and Israel’s Election

Donald Trump spent Sunday conducting four foreign policies at once. Iran should surrender. Oman could be bombed. Hamas is supposedly disarming. Israeli elections are none of his business, unless he chooses a candidate.

The president returned from New Jersey saying he had a “great weekend” with “a lot of meetings,” but refused to say whether Iran had been discussed. 

Hours later, he posted that Iran must never be allowed to possess a nuclear weapon “in any way, shape, or form.” Silence at the airport, capital letters online, threats on television.

In a Fox News interview, Trump said Iran should “put up the white flag of surrender.” He said he had no deadline and was “not in a hurry,” dismissing the idea that U.S. midterm elections would affect his decisions. Iran, he said, was full of “good poker players,” but was “dying.” 

Trump also claimed Washington has a secret backchannel with senior Islamic Revolutionary Guard Corps officials. Iran denied it. An IRGC spokesman called the claim a product of Trump’s “illusions and nightmares” after U.S. failure in the war. 

The reported channel is now either a diplomatic breakthrough or a fantasy, depending on which capital is speaking.

Oman received a threat, not mediation. As Muscat negotiates with Tehran over arrangements in the Strait of Hormuz, Trump said that if Oman “gets in the way,” the United States would “bomb the shit out of them.” 

Oman has been one of Washington’s most useful regional intermediaries for decades. The reward for mediation is apparently to be threatened on Fox News. 

On Gaza, Trump told Israel to avoid further attacks because Hamas had agreed to lay down its weapons. “We have our own relationship with Hamas,” he said. “They are giving up their guns.” Hamas spokesman Hazem Qassem welcomed the remarks and urged Trump to pressure Israel to honor the next phase of the peace plan. 

Then Trump addressed Israeli politics with the evasive skill of a man who has already decided he wants to be asked. “I think it’s most appropriate for me to stay out of Israeli elections,” he said. “But I may endorse somebody.” 

That is not noninterference. It is a public auction for relevance.

Former congresswoman Marjorie Taylor Greene added to the confusion, claiming without public evidence that the administration had discussed using nuclear weapons against Iran in strategy meetings. The White House has not confirmed the claim. 

Trump’s diplomatic style is simple. He offers surrender, a backchannel, a threat and an endorsement. Each feature activates when the microphone is on.
